title: Storing passwords
context: How should a backend store user passwords?

source.title: JavaGuide (Snailclimb): Spring knowledge and questions
source.note: Question and topic from this JavaGuide article. The answer is an original English write-up; see content/sources/javaguide/NOTICE.md.

answer: Never store plain text, and don't use fast hashes like MD5 or SHA-256 alone, because they can be brute-forced quickly. Use a slow, salted password hash designed for passwords: BCrypt, SCrypt, PBKDF2 or Argon2. In Spring Security, `PasswordEncoder` with `DelegatingPasswordEncoder` does this and lets you upgrade algorithms later. Compare with `matches`, never by hashing and comparing strings yourself. Encryption, which you can reverse, is the wrong tool for passwords.

points.title: Slow salted hash
points.why: A salted, slow hash resists brute force. Fast hashes don't.

points.title: Use PasswordEncoder
points.why: Spring Security's PasswordEncoder handles salts and lets you migrate algorithms.
